questiontext.text: What is a common problem in large programs written in a Procedural style, where data is scattered and functions are disconnected?

generalfeedback.text: Procedural programming lacks a way to bundle data with the logic that acts upon it, leading to organizational challenges in large projects.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modularity is typically a strength of OOP, not a problem of Procedural code.
Correct! Without clear object boundaries, changes in one part of the code often break unrelated parts.
Incorrect. Typing issues are independent of the programming paradigm (Procedural vs OOP).
Incorrect. Procedural programming does not use classes by definition.

questiontext.text: Which keyword is used to start a new class definition in Python?

generalfeedback.text: The class keyword tells the Python interpreter that we are defining a new blueprint.

feedback.text: Incorrect. def is used to define functions and methods.
Correct! This keyword initializes the definition of a new type.
Incorrect. object is a base class name, not a keyword for definition.
Incorrect. interface is a keyword in Java, but not in Python.

questiontext.text: Consider r1 = Robot() and r2 = Robot(). What will r1 == r2 return by default (if __eq__ is not overridden)?

generalfeedback.text: By default, Python checks if two variables point to the same location in memory (identity), not if they contain the same data.

answer.text: True, because they belong to the same class.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Belonging to the same class does not make two distinct objects equal.

answer.text: False, because they are different objects in memory.

feedback.text: Correct! Even if their attributes are identical, they are two separate instances.
Incorrect. Comparison operations always return a boolean (True/False).
Incorrect. Comparing objects is valid syntax.

questiontext.text: What is the purpose of the dot operator (.) in Python OOP?

generalfeedback.text: The dot operator is the primary way to interact with an object's internals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. def is used for definitions.

answer.text: To access attributes and methods of an object.

feedback.text: Correct! It connects the object instance to its data and behavior.
Incorrect. The / operator is used for division.
Incorrect. The + operator or f-strings are used for concatenation.

questiontext.text: Inside a method, how must you refer to an attribute battery belonging to the current instance?

generalfeedback.text: Without self, Python looks for a local variable within the method, not an instance attribute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This would refer to a local variable named battery.
Correct! self tells Python to look in the object's own namespace.
Incorrect. Unless a variable named robot is passed in, this will raise a NameError.
Incorrect. this is not a standard keyword in Python.

questiontext.text: Can the __init__ method have default values for its parameters?

generalfeedback.text: Default parameters make classes more flexible by allowing instantiation with minimal information.

answer.text: Yes, it behaves like a normal method/function in this regard.

feedback.text: Correct! You can provide defaults just like in any other Python function.

answer.text: No, all parameters in __init__ must be provided during instantiation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Defaults are fully supported and widely used.

answer.text: Only if the class inherits from ABC.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This feature is available to all classes.
Incorrect. The self parameter should never have a default value provided by the user.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a common practice inside the __init__ method?

generalfeedback.text: The constructor is the gatekeeper of an object's state.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Global variables defeat the purpose of encapsulation in OOP.
Correct! Ensuring that attributes like radius are not negative at creation is good practice.

answer.text: Looping through all existing objects of the class.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An object typically doesn't know about other instances of the same class at creation.
Incorrect. Imports should generally be at the top of the file, not inside a constructor.

questiontext.text: What is another common name for a Child Class in inheritance?

generalfeedback.text: Different textbooks use different terms, but the relationship remains the same.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This refers to the Parent Class.
Correct! It is "derived" from an existing class.
Incorrect. This refers to the Parent Class.
Incorrect. While conceptually similar, "Ancestor" is not a standard technical term in OOP inheritance.

questiontext.text: If a child class Truck inherits from Vehicle, and defines a new method load_cargo(), can an instance of the parent Vehicle call this method?

generalfeedback.text: Inheritance is a one-way street: children know about parents, but parents don't know about specialized children.

answer.text: Yes, parents inherit from their children.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inheritance works downwards, from parent to child.

answer.text: No, specific functionality in the child is not available to the parent.

feedback.text: Correct! A generic Vehicle does not know how to load cargo like a Truck does.

answer.text: Only if the method is marked as public.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Even public methods of a child are unknown to the parent class definition.

answer.text: Yes, if the Truck object was created before the Vehicle object.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The creation order of objects does not change class definitions.

questiontext.text: In Python 3, what is the built-in base class that all classes automatically inherit from?

generalfeedback.text: The object class provides default behaviors like string conversion and equality checks that all objects share.

feedback.text: Incorrect. While common in some frameworks, it is not the Python built-in name.
Correct! class MyClass: is shorthand for class MyClass(object):.
Incorrect. This is not the built-in name.
Incorrect. This is not the built-in name.

questiontext.text: What does the "Closed for Modification" part of the Open/Closed Principle mean?

generalfeedback.text: The goal is to build software that can grow without requiring risky changes to existing, tested code.

answer.text: You should never update your software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Software must always evolve; the principle is about how it evolves.

answer.text: You shouldn't have to change existing, working code to add new functionality (e.g., adding a new vehicle type).

feedback.text: Correct! You extend the system by adding new classes, not by modifying core loops.

answer.text: The source code should be hidden from users.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This refers to proprietary software or encapsulation, but not this specific principle.
Incorrect. This is Encapsulation, which supports the Open/Closed principle but is not the principle itself.

questiontext.text: What is the meaning of a single underscore prefix (e.g., _pin) for a variable name in Python?

generalfeedback.text: In Python, "we are all consenting adults." Privacy is enforced by consensus and convention, not by the compiler.

answer.text: The variable is completely private and cannot be accessed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python technically allows access; it's just a warning to developers.

answer.text: It is a convention indicating "internal use"; developers should avoid accessing it from outside.

feedback.text: Correct! It's a "Keep Out" sign for other programmers.

answer.text: The variable is a constant and cannot be changed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Constants are written in ALL_CAPS.

answer.text: The variable is automatically synchronized with a database.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is not a built-in Python behavior.

questiontext.text: What mechanism does Python use when it sees a double underscore prefix (__attribute) to make it harder to access from outside the class?

generalfeedback.text: Name mangling changes __attr to _ClassName__attr to prevent accidental overrides in child classes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The data is not encrypted; the name is just changed.
Correct! This is the technical term for this Python-specific behavior.
Incorrect. "Data Hiding" is the conceptual goal, but "Name Mangling" is the mechanism.
Incorrect. The attribute is not deleted; it's renamed.

questiontext.text: Which concept allows you to define a "virtual" attribute that is calculated on the fly rather than stored as a fixed value?

generalfeedback.text: Computed properties ensure that dependent data (like area) is always synchronized with primary data (like width and height).

feedback.text: Incorrect. Static variables are fixed and shared across instances.
Correct! It looks like an attribute to the user but runs a method internally.
Incorrect. These are not part of an object and don't provide the attribute-like syntax.
Incorrect. Constructors only run at the moment of object creation.

questiontext.text: Why is Composition considered more flexible than Inheritance for building a "Car" with an "Engine"?

generalfeedback.text: Composition avoids the "Diamond Problem" and deep hierarchies, making the system modular.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Composition might actually use slightly more memory as you have more separate objects.

answer.text: You can easily swap out the engine (e.g., from Gas to Electric) without changing the Car class.

feedback.text: Correct! This is the essence of modular design.

answer.text: It allows the Car to access private variables of the Engine.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Composition actually enforces better boundaries; the Car can only use the Engine's public interface.

answer.text: It makes the Car a subtype of the Engine.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This would be Inheritance, and it's logically wrong (a Car is not a subtype of an Engine).
